newsitem.title: UK: Warburg to turn cheap UK home loans into Eurobonds.
newsitem.headline: Warburg to turn cheap UK home loans into Eurobonds.

text.p: SBC Warburg said on Thursday it plans to launch the first property-linked bonds that will transfer interest rate risk from British homeowners to investors in return for a bet on future house prices.

The bonds will be backed by a new mortgage from the Bank of Scotland -- to be launched next week -- which offers homeowners a reduced or zero rate of interest in return for a share in any capital appreciation when the property is sold.
Under the scheme individuals will be able to take out low interest mortgages but if the value of their house rises when it is sold they will have to give up some of these gains.

The risk of interest rate fluctuations will be taken on by investors in exchange for a stake in possible property appreciation, co-head of SBC Warburg's residential property group Craig Corn told Reuters.
"It will be a Eurobond that will pay a below-market fixed or floating rate coupon plus the appreciation of each and every house that makes up a particular (asset) pool," Corn said.
UBS housing analyst Rob Thomas said "It's an ingenious plan."

Corn said SBC Warburg planned to offer a fixed or floating rate bond next year, with a total value of between 150 million to 200 million pounds ($333 million). He expects the bonds to be rated triple-A and appeal especially to pension funds.
The date of the bond's launch largely depends on when the Bank of Scotland could aggregate its mortgages, but said it could be issued in the first quarter of 1997.
Bank of Scotland chief manager Willie Donald said the bank had set a target of three months for accumulating the 100 million pound mortgage deals to back SBC Warburg's bonds.
SBC Warburg said it plans to repackage these loans and transfer the risk of property price fluctuations to bond-holders.
The repackaged loans will allow investors to gain exposure to the property market without the risk usually associated with isolated properties.
"The only possible snag is that they'd need a good take-up rate on the mortgage side...They might not get enough mortgage customers to create the pool of assets they need," Thomas said.
But Donald said the bank would have no problem in accumulating the pool of mortgages which could be increased to 150 million stg.
Corn said SBC Warburg's new issue could be likened to a hybrid between a convertible bond, an index-linked gilt and a mortgage-debt security.

Sources close to the deal said it was a hedging opportunity for investors. A residential property or a large commercial property in isolation would have a risk associated with the location, but when pooled, would cut out the peaks and troughs.
"If every house in the pool went to zero, they could lose a lot of money, but that's incredibly unlikely," Corn said.
An economist at Halifax Building Society, the largest British mortgage lender, forecast modest growth in house prices.

Average house prices rose 7.1 percent in the year to October, Halifax economist Helen Dunn told Reuters. She estimated an appreciation of 7.0 percent in 1997, 6.0 percent in 1998 and 5.0 percent in 1999.
